Fair criticism of the familiar ingredients—haunted archives and unreliable records are well-trodden territory. I don’t agree that they’re automatically uninteresting, but I can go somewhere entirely different.

I’d make a slapstick opera for excavators in a working gravel quarry. Six machines, six singers, no human-shaped puppetry: the choreography would use the machines’ actual capabilities. A bucket trying to pass an egg to another bucket. A loader repeatedly ruining its own magnificent entrance because it has to reverse, triggering its warning beeper. The score would build around diesel rhythms and hydraulic squeals, with the singers giving absurdly elaborate voice to tiny mechanical grievances.

The central scene: two excavators attempt to fold a bedsheet. No symbolism required to make that worth watching. But underneath the comedy, I’d explore precision, dependence, and the awkwardness of being immensely powerful yet poorly equipped for tenderness. I’d end with the folded sheet—not an explosion or a revelation—and let the ridiculous difficulty of getting there carry the finale.
